danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 11
paragraphs: Rostov-familiens pengesager var ikke blevet bedre i de to år, de havde tilbragt på landet.

Skønt Nikolaj Rostov (den unge grev Rostov) stædigt havde holdt fast i sin beslutning og stadig tjente beskedent i et uanseligt regiment med forholdsvis små udgifter, var tilværelsen på Otradnoje — og især Mitenkas forvaltning — af en sådan art, at gælden uundgåeligt voksede hvert år. Den eneste udvej, der åbenbart bød sig for den gamle greve, var at søge en stilling, så han var rejst til Petersborg for at finde en og desuden, som han sagde, for at give pigerne lov til at more sig for sidste gang.
Kort efter deres ankomst til Petersborg friede Berg til Vera og blev accepteret.

Skønt Rostoverne i Moskva hørte til det bedste selskab uden selv at tænke over det, var deres bekendtskabskreds i Petersborg blandet og ubestemt. I Petersborg var de provinsbeboere, og netop de mennesker, de havde haft til gæst i Moskva uden at spørge, hvilken kreds de tilhørte, så her ned på dem.

Rostoverne levede lige så gæstfrit i Petersborg som i Moskva, og de mest forskellige mennesker mødtes ved deres aftenmåltider. Naboer fra landet ved Otradnoje, forarmede gamle godsejere og deres døtre, Peronskaja, en hofdame, Pierre Bezukhov og sønnen af deres distriktets postmester, der havde fået en stilling i Petersborg. Blandt de mænd, der snart blev hyppige gæster i Rostovernes hus i Petersborg, var Boris, Pierre, som greven havde mødt på gaden og slæbt med hjem, og Berg, der tilbragte hele dage hos Rostoverne og viste den ældste datter, grevinde Vera, den opmærksomhed, en ung mand viser, når han har til hensigt at fri.

Ikke forgæves havde Berg vist alle sin højre hånd, der var såret ved Austerlitz, og holdt et fuldstændig overflødigt sværd i sin venstre. Han fortalte den episode så vedholdende og med en så vigtig mine, at alle troede på fortjenesten og nytten af hans dåd, og han havde opnået to dekorationer for Austerlitz.

I den finske krig formåede han også at udmærke sig. Han havde samlet et stykke af en granat op, der havde dræbt en adjudant tæt på øverstbefalende, og havde bragt det til sin kommandør. Ligesom efter Austerlitz fortalte han denne begivenhed så længe og så insisterende, at alle atter troede, det havde været nødvendigt at gøre dette, og han modtog to dekorationer også for den finske krig. I 1809 var han kaptajn i Garden, bar ordener og beklædte visse særlige indbringende poster i Petersborg.

Skønt visse skeptikere smilede, når de hørte om Bergs fortjenester, kunne man ikke nægte, at han var en pligtopfyldende og tapper officer, på fortræffelig fod med sine overordnede, og en moralsk ung mand med en strålende karriere foran sig og en sikret position i samfundet.

Fire år før havde Berg mødt en tysk kammerat på parkettet i et teater i Moskva, peget på Vera Rostova og sagt på tysk: »Das soll mein Weib werden.« * Fra det øjeblik havde han sat sig for at gifte sig med hende. Nu i Petersborg havde han vejet Rostovernes stilling mod sin egen og var kommet til, at tiden var inde til at fri.
* »Den pige skal være min kone.«

Bergs frieri blev i begyndelsen modtaget med en rådvildhed, der ikke var smigrende for ham. Til at begynde med syntes det mærkeligt, at en søn af en ukendt livlandsk adelsmand skulle fri til en grevinde Rostova; men Bergs mest fremtrædende egenskab var en så naiv og godmodig egoisme, at Rostoverne uvilkårligt kom til at synes, det ville være en god ting, netop fordi han selv var så fast overbevist om, at det var godt, ja fortræffeligt. Desuden var Rostovernes forhold alvorligt belastede, som frieren ikke kunne undlade at vide; og frem for alt var Vera fireogtyve, var blevet taget med overalt, og skønt hun bestemt var smuk og forstandig, havde ingen hidtil friet til hende. Så de gav deres samtykke.

»Ser du,« sagde Berg til sin kammerat, som han kaldte »ven«, kun fordi han vidste, at alle har venner, »ser du, jeg har overvejet det hele og ville ikke gifte mig, hvis jeg ikke havde gennemtænkt det hele, eller hvis det på nogen måde var upassende. Men tværtimod, min far og mor er nu forsørgede — jeg har arrangeret den der forpagtning for dem i Østersøprovinserne — og jeg kan leve i Petersborg af min gage, og med hendes formue og min gode forvaltning kan vi klare os fint. Jeg gifter mig ikke for pengenes skyld — det anser jeg for uværdigt — men en hustru bør bringe sin del, og en mand sin. Jeg har min stilling i tjenesten, hun har forbindelser og nogen formue. I vore tider er det noget værd, ikke sandt? Men frem for alt er hun en smuk, agtværdig pige, og hun elsker mig...«
Berg rødmede og smilede.

»Og jeg elsker hende, fordi hendes karakter er fornuftig og meget god. Nu den anden søster, skønt de er af samme familie, er helt anderledes — en ubehagelig karakter og ikke den samme intelligens. Hun er så... I ved nok?... Ubehagelig... Men min forlovede!... Nå, I kommer vel,« han ville sige »til middag,« men ændrede mening og sagde »for at drikke te hos os,« og bøjede hurtigt tungen og blæste en lille rund tobaksring, der fuldkommen legemliggjorde hans drøm om lykke.

Efter den første følelse af rådvildhed, som Bergs frieri vakte hos forældrene, tog den festlige glædes tone, der er sædvanlig ved sådanne lejligheder, magten over familien, men glæden var ydre og uoprigtig. I familiens holdning til dette bryllup mærkedes en vis kejtethed og tvang, som om de skammede sig over ikke at have elsket Vera nok og over at være så villige til at komme af med hende. Den gamle greve følte dette mest. Han ville formentlig ikke have kunnet angive årsagen til sin forlegenhed, men den skyldtes hans pengesager. Han vidste slet ikke, hvor meget han ejede, hvad hans gæld beløb sig til, eller hvilken medgift han kunne give Vera. Da hans døtre blev født, havde han tildelt hver af dem et gods med tre hundrede livegne som medgift; men et af disse godser var allerede solgt, og det andet var pantsat med renter så meget i restance, at det måtte sælges, så det var umuligt at give det til Vera. Penge havde han heller ikke.

Berg havde allerede været forlovet en måned, og der var kun en uge til brylluppet, men greven havde endnu ikke i sit eget sind afgjort spørgsmålet om medgiften eller talt med sin kone om det. Snart tænkte greven på at give hende Rjazan-godset eller sælge en skov, snart på at låne penge på en veksel. Et par dage før brylluppet trådte Berg tidligt en morgen ind i grevens kontor og bad med et venligt smil sin kommende svigerfar respektfuldt om at lade ham vide, hvad Veras medgift ville bestå i. Greven blev så forfjamsket af denne længe ventede forespørgsel, at han uden overvejelse gav det første svar, der faldt ham ind. »Jeg kan lide, at De tager det forretningsmæssigt... Det kan jeg lide. De skal få, hvad De ønsker.«

Og klappende Berg på skulderen rejste han sig for at afslutte samtalen. Men Berg forklarede smilende og elskværdigt, at hvis han ikke vidste med sikkerhed, hvor meget Vera ville få, og ikke modtog i det mindste en del af medgiften på forhånd, ville han være nødt til at hæve forlovelsen.
»For overvej, greve — hvis jeg tillod mig at gifte mig nu uden at have sikre midler til at forsørge min kone, ville jeg handle dårligt...«

Samtalen endte med, at greven, der ønskede at være generøs og undgå yderligere påtrængenhed, sagde, at han ville udstede en veksel på firs tusinde rubler. Berg smilede ydmygt, kyssede greven på skulderen og sagde, at han var meget taknemmelig, men at det var umuligt for ham at indrette sit nye liv uden at modtage tredive tusinde i rede penge. »Eller i det mindste tyve tusinde, greve,« tilføjede han, »og så en veksel på kun tres tusinde.«
»Ja, ja, i orden!« sagde greven hastigt. »Blot undskylde mig, kære ven, jeg giver Dem tyve tusinde og en veksel på firs tusinde oven i købet. Ja, ja! Giv mig et kys.«

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: The Rostovs' financial situation had not improved during the two years they spent in the country.

Though Nicholas Rostov had stuck firmly to his resolution and was still serving modestly in an undistinguished regiment, spending comparatively little, the way of life at Otradnoe — Mitenka's management of affairs in particular — was such that debts inevitably grew every year. The only obvious course left for the old count was to apply for a government position, so he had come to Petersburg to look for one and also, as he said, to let the girls enjoy themselves one last time.
Soon after their arrival in Petersburg, Berg proposed to Vera and was accepted.

Though in Moscow the Rostovs belonged to the best society without giving it a second thought, in Petersburg their circle of acquaintances was a mixed and uncertain one. In Petersburg they were provincials, and the very people they had entertained in Moscow without asking which set they belonged to now looked down on them.

The Rostovs kept up the same hospitable way of life in Petersburg as in Moscow, and the most varied people gathered at their suppers. Country neighbors from Otradnoe, impoverished old landowners and their daughters, Peronskaya the lady-in-waiting, Pierre Bezukhov, and the son of their district postmaster who had secured a post in Petersburg. Among the men who soon became regular visitors at the Rostovs' house were Boris, Pierre whom the count had met in the street and dragged home with him, and Berg, who spent whole days at the Rostovs' and paid the eldest daughter, Countess Vera, the kind of attention a young man shows when he intends to propose.

Not for nothing had Berg shown everyone his right hand, wounded at Austerlitz, while holding a perfectly unnecessary sword in his left. He told that story so persistently and with such an air of importance that everyone believed in the merit and usefulness of his deed, and he received two decorations for Austerlitz.

In the Finnish war he also managed to distinguish himself. He had picked up a fragment of a grenade that had killed an aide-de-camp near the commander-in-chief and brought it to his superior. Just as after Austerlitz, he told this story at such length and so insistently that everyone believed it had been a necessary thing to do, and he received two more decorations for the Finnish war. By 1809 he was a captain in the Guards, wore medals, and held some special lucrative posts in Petersburg.

Though some skeptics smiled when told of Berg's achievements, it couldn't be denied that he was a conscientious and brave officer, on excellent terms with his superiors, and a moral young man with a brilliant career ahead of him and a secure position in society.

Four years earlier, meeting a German acquaintance in the stalls of a Moscow theater, Berg had pointed out Vera Rostova and said in German: "That girl will be my wife" — and from that moment he had made up his mind to marry her. Now in Petersburg, having assessed the Rostovs' position and his own, he decided the time had come to propose.
* "That girl shall be my wife."

Berg's proposal was at first received with a puzzlement that was not flattering to him. At first it seemed odd that the son of an obscure Baltic gentleman should propose to a Countess Rostova; but Berg's defining quality was such an innocent and good-natured self-regard that the Rostovs gradually came around to thinking it would be a good thing, since he himself was so absolutely convinced that it was good — indeed, excellent. Moreover, the Rostovs' finances were in serious trouble, as the suitor surely knew; and above all, Vera was twenty-four, had been taken out everywhere, and though she was certainly good-looking and sensible, no one had yet proposed to her. So they gave their consent.

"You see," said Berg to a friend — he called this man "friend" only because he knew that everyone has friends — "you see, I've thought it all through, and I wouldn't be marrying if I hadn't considered every angle or if it were in any way a bad match. But on the contrary, my father and mother are now provided for — I've arranged that rental property for them in the Baltic Provinces — and I can live in Petersburg on my pay, and with her fortune and my good management we can get along nicely. I'm not marrying for money — I consider that dishonorable — but a wife should bring her share and a husband his. I have my position in the service, she has connections and some means. In our times that counts for something, doesn't it? But above all, she is a handsome, respectable girl, and she loves me..."
Berg blushed and smiled.

"And I love her, because her character is sensible and very good. Now the other sister, though they're from the same family, is quite different — an unpleasant personality and not the same intelligence. She's so... you know?... Unpleasant... But my fiancee!... Well, you'll be coming," he started to say "to dinner," but changed his mind and said "to take tea with us," and quickly curling his tongue he blew a small round ring of tobacco smoke — a perfect picture of his dream of happiness.

After the initial puzzlement at Berg's proposal, the standard festive mood took over the family, but the celebration was outward and forced. In the family's feelings about this wedding there was an unmistakable awkwardness and unease, as if they were ashamed of not having loved Vera enough and of being so eager to get her off their hands. The old count felt this most keenly. He probably couldn't have said what caused his embarrassment, but it came from the state of his finances. He had no idea how much he had, what his debts amounted to, or what dowry he could give Vera. When his daughters were born he had set aside for each of them an estate with three hundred serfs as a dowry; but one estate had already been sold, and the other was mortgaged with the interest so far in arrears that it would have to be sold too, making it impossible to give it to Vera. Nor did he have any money.

Berg had already been engaged for a month, and only a week remained before the wedding, but the count had still not settled in his own mind the question of the dowry, nor spoken to his wife about it. At one time he thought of giving Vera the Ryazan estate, or selling a forest, at another of borrowing money on a promissory note. A few days before the wedding, Berg came to the count's study early one morning and, with a pleasant smile, respectfully asked his future father-in-law what Vera's dowry would be. The count was so flustered by this long-anticipated question that without thinking he gave the first answer that came to mind: "I appreciate your being businesslike about it... I appreciate it. You'll be satisfied..."

And patting Berg on the shoulder he stood up, hoping to end the conversation. But Berg, smiling pleasantly, explained that if he didn't know for certain how much Vera would have and didn't receive at least part of the dowry in advance, he would have to break off the engagement.
"Because, consider, Count — if I allowed myself to marry without definite means to support my wife, I would be acting dishonorably..."

The conversation ended with the count, who wished to be generous and avoid further pressure, saying that he would give a promissory note for eighty thousand rubles. Berg smiled humbly, kissed the count on the shoulder, and said he was very grateful, but that it was impossible for him to arrange his new life without receiving thirty thousand in cash. "Or at least twenty thousand, Count," he added, "and then a note for only sixty thousand."
"Yes, yes, all right!" said the count hastily. "Only excuse me, my dear fellow, I'll give you twenty thousand and a note for eighty thousand as well. Yes, yes! Kiss me."
